speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROPOSED FIVE PER CENT TAX ON INTEREST AND DIVIDEND PAYMENTS TO NON-RESIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the introduction of any new tax there is bound at its inception to be some confusion, if only in getting the mechanics into proper and smooth operation. That difficulty is accentuated in the case of bearer bonds which are held in varying amounts by large numbers of people throughout the world. Having that in mind the commissioner of income tax on March 23 prepared a document entitled "A brief interim summary of the budget proposals with respect to ownership certificates and deduction of the five per cent tax at the source." Several

hundreds of these have been circulated to the Canadian banks and to certain financial and trust companies in Canada. They have also been forwarded in ample time to New York, and to-day they arrive in the city of London, England, with instructions that they be reprinted there in French for circulation in France. One paragraph only of this document I desire to read:
There is no deduction in respect of interest paid on bonds of Dominion of Canada issued free of income tax or upon interest on bonds paid by the Canadian National Railways wherein the Canadian National Railways or any of its subsidiaries undertakes to pay any tax imposed Upon the holder thereof, these payments requiring no covering ownership certificates, either forms 600 or 601.
I desire in addition to make it very clear that it is not intended that the five per cent tax shall apply in the case of a foreign holder of a bond of the Dominion of Canada which in terms provides that the dominion shall pay an amount certain; also in the case of British or foreign non-resident holders of bearer coupons and share warrants, unless the holder requests an ownership certificate, such coupon and share warrants may be cashed without the necessity of ownership certificates being attached. It is understood, however, that the five per cent tax must be withheld by the paying agent.
Of necessity these documents had to be printed somewhat hurriedly, and as a sufficient number is not available at the moment for every hon. member of the house, I desire to lay on the table -two copies in English, stating at the same time that as soon as possible a larger number will be available both in English and French. I desire also for the information of the house to lay on the table in English and French specimen copies of the ownership certificates which will be required to be attached to these documents.

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minster of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 53, to amend the criminal code (offensive weapons).
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
On section 1-Offensive weapons.
Mr. LAPOINTE':	May I ask the minister
whether this bill is the same that was passed by the Senate on two or three occasions in recent years?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
No. I believe this bill
has originated in the Department of Justice in response to many requests which have come from municipal bodies, boards of trade and various other societies throughout Canada, asking that more drastic legislation be passed in regard to the use or carrying of pistols and revolvers. Requests which from time to time have come in have been very sweeping, and the penalties which we have been requested to impose have been very severe. However, after consultation with the law officers of the Department of Justice, with representatives of the various police associations and with the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police it has been decided to introduce the present measure, particularly directed against pistols and revolvers on the

one hand and offensive weapons on the other. In the bill there is a distinction between pistols and revolvers and what are known as offensive weapons. The term "offensive weapon" is defined in the criminal code as follows:
"Offensive weapon" or "weapon" includes any gnn or other fire arm, or air-gun, or any part thereof, or any sword, sword blade, bayonet, pike, pike-head, spear, spear-head, dirk, dagger, knife, or other instrument intended for cutting or stabbing, or any metal knuckles, or other deadly or dangerous weapon, and any instrument or thing intended to be used as a weapon, and all ammunition which may be used with or for any weapon.
We are maintaining the clauses against the use of offensive weapons, but are presenting new clauses in regard to pistols and revolvers as distinct from other offensive weapons. One request which has come from all quarters of Canad'a is that we should pass an enactment in the House of Commons to prevent the importation, manufacture and sale of pistols and revolvers. As the house will readily understand, if we were to attempt legislation of that kind we should immediately be confronted with constitutional difficulties. However it is perhaps some satisfaction to know that the question of the importation of such weapons is at the present time subject to permit; such weapons cannot be imported into Canada to-day without a permit issued by the Department of National Revenue. On the other hand it must give some satisfaction to know that to-day there is no manufacture whatever of pistols or revolvers in the Dominion of Canada. So that at the present time we are relieved from any difficulty on that score.
The other matter is one of sale, namely whether or not we have the power to prevent sale within the provinces. That is a nice question. In this bill we have sought to regulate the sale, without actually prohibiting it, and we believe that in the regulations proposed in the bill we are within our constitutional rights. There are some amendments which will have to be offered as the bill proceeds, and I think as we have now reached the first section we might mention the first amendment which presents itself.
The penalty imposed by the first section for the carrying of a pistol or revolver is a term of imprisonment of five years. I think the house will agree that the penalty is rather severe. Five years or more was the penalty suggested by the petitioners, but on this section I propose to ask that it be amended by fixing the term at from one to not more than five years, thereby giving the court or judge some discretion in the matter.

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Is it within the discretion
of the magistrate or the court to impose a sentence of less than a year, or can he pass a suspended sentence, or anything of that sort?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Of course a judge has
power to suspend sentence, unless we take away that power. But the idea was that a man who is carrying 'concealed weapons should be subject to a term of one year for the offence but not more than five. I am sorry to say that according to the reports from the police associations of various cities in Canada the number of persons found carrying pistols and revolvers has in recent years very largely increased. It is the commonest thing now when a man is arrested for crime, upon searching him in the police court, to discover that he has in his possession a pistol or revolver. He may be a man with a long criminal record. The present penalties for carrying such a weapon are not considered very severe. It is felt that if restrictions are placed upon the sale, and greater penalties are imposed for the offence of carrying, the traffic in these weapons will at least be considerably diminished.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Section 1 replaces eleven sections of the criminal code by new sections. I suggest that we should take every section individually.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: It does not replace them all by new sections. Many are just repetitions of the old.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: But it is better to adopt each one separately.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I understand this action is being taken largely on the recommendation of the various police associations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: No; I did not intend to convey that idea. I consulted some police associations, but the action is taken on the representation of city councils, boards of trade and other organizations of the kind throughout Canada.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to making the law as stringent as may be necessary, with regard to the carrying of arms. But there is one point I should like to raise, and it is this: What sort of regulation is there with regard to the carrying of revolvers and pistols by the police themselves? In the old country, as a good many know, the ordinary police constables do not carry revolvers. They have batons merely. A few days ago in the city of Montreal there was brought to our notice an outrageous case of
a man being shot during the course of an eviction. I understand he was shot in the back by a police constable named Zappa. According to the press it seems there was a man there who had got behind in his rent owing to the compensation board not being prompt in paying him, and he was being evicted. A boarder went to the house to rescue some of his own personal belongings. Just what took place is not clear; according to the police he resisted; according to bystanders he had nothing whatever in his hand, and made no resistance. However, the fact is he was shot. Later there was a most disgraceful scene: It seems to be established by the reports of nearly all the papers in Montreal that at the time of the funeral, when some of the friends and sympathizers of the man who had thus been shot were proceeding with the cortege, the police intervened and broke up the funeral procession, using extreme violence, women and children being brutally knocked down. There was said by the papers to be no riot whatever and nothing in the way of disorder in the procession until the police intervened. That particular incident, to which a great deal of publicity was given in all the Montreal papers, both English and French, seems to point to the need of some supervision of the police themselves. If we are going to insist, as I think we should, that ordinary civilians do not go around armed with revolvers, I do not think it is fair that the police should be armed without having definite restrictions placed upon them. As I said a while ago, we talk about British traditions; police constables in England are not armed, they are in the United States, and apparently we are introducing that kind of thing here. I submit that one of the reasons we have armed criminals in this country is that they know they have to deal with constables who are armed with lethal weapons. I would like to see the government hold the police responsible.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
May it be the reverse,
that the police are armed because so many people are armed?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Well, I do not want to be misunderstood-I hope this measure passes. At the same time I think there ought to be very much more definite control of the police themselves. That one instance of a man shot in the back without any clear evidence that he was resisting arrest is sufficient, I think, to make any one who has any idea of British traditions rebel against the idea of the police being given such a free hand. This policeman, according to his own

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
statement, became angry and shot the man. We have courts to decide whether or not a man is guilty, and we have certain officers charged with executing judgment, but certainly the task of the police is not that of judge and executioner. If a man is to be killed let him be executed after his case has gone through the regular judicial process.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
After he has been
shot.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
No, not after he
is shot. Of course the police ought to be protected and to have a fair break, but I submit that in the drafting of this legislation there should be some provision by which guns should not be permitted even to the police except under strict supervision, the police being made definitely responsible for their use. I would say that the policeman who shoots a man in the back, I do not care if he is an officer, is cowardly, and you are not going to get respect for the law as long as the police are allowed liberty of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
If the question was
addressed to me, I may say that the control of provincial police and municipal police is strictly within the powers of the various provincial governments. The provisions of this bill as it is drafted apply to all persons, but there is a provision therein that permits for the carrying of revolvers for the protection of life and property may be granted by the attorneys general of the various provinces, and if in the judgment of the provincial authorities police forces should not be armed they will not be armed. On the other hand if the various provincial authorities think their police forces should be armed they can grant the necessary permits. But that is hardly a matter that concerns this federal parliament. We have not sought in any way to interfere with the jurisdiction either of the municipalities or of the provinces in respect to police matters.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
But I think that
hardly answers my point. This is general legislation applying to every citizen, every individual in this country. We have here still another example of division of jurisdiction. This is federal legislation, yet when it comes to dealing with the particular class that we call police constables we are told that it is entirely a provincial matter, I think the body that legislates on behalf of the great mass of the people should also provide adequate restrictions for the granting of permits even to police officers.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
The minister's remarks regarding provincial authority over their own police may be quite in order. Yet we have at this time a decided growth in the duties and work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which is taking over police jurisdiction in various localities. I believe that every one in this house is thoroughly in accord with any legislation designed to prohibit the carrying of concealed weapons. It is an evil which we have acquired from our neighbours to the south. None of us believes in it in any way, shape or form. Only a very few decades ago you would not find a policeman on the streets of any American or Canadian city with the two gun holsters exposed. The whole business of gun carrying has been much increased simply by the ostentatious display of weapons by the police. Of late years the Ontario provincial police have gone to an absolutely absurd length in this regard. In small towns and country districts all through Ontario, for the first time in history we now see provincial police going around with a holster and two exposed guns. The thing is absurd from any angle. There are no dangerous criminals in the rural districts of Ontario, and the duties of our police do not demand the carrying of either concealed or exposed weapons. The idea of using guns in dealing with thugs and gunmen in some of the large cities may be quite justified, but the work performed by the provincial police of Ontario does not demand the use of weapons.
I thoroughly agree with the general remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the carrying of revolvers by police, which is an American system absolutely opposed to the whole idea of police methods in Great Britain, has induced the use of revolvers by a great many people who have no need of them. I do submit to the Minister of Justice that the department of police over which he has jurisdiction, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, have erred very little in the display of revolvers, and I hope the minister will see that they continue this practice. It does seem to me, however, that when the mounted police can do their work without the use of firearms the minister would be quite justified in asking the provincial governments to pass concurrent legislation to prevent their police forces from making such a display of firearms as we see throughout the country today.

speechtext:
In justice to the government of Quebec which is charged with the maintenance of law and order in that province I should like to say that yesterday in the

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
legislature the premier, referring to the case *to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has alluded, declared that the matter had been fully investigated by a judge of the sessions in Montreal as well as by a coroner's jury, and that in both cases this policeman had been exonerated from any blame in the matter. I do not know anything of the matter more than that. It was also stated yesterday, and endorsed by the leader of the opposition in the legislature, that the laws for the maintenance of order in the province of Quebec would be revised in order to give some protection to the citizens of 'that province against the actions of the foreign element which has come to Quebec in the last few years. This brings the matter to a head. Our province has had the reputation of being very peaceful and law-abiding; everyone wants it to remain so, but those who read the Montreal papers no doubt are aware that there is a very strong communistic element now established in that city, and certain things which have occurred lately have brought this matter to the attention of the government, who intend to deal with it.
With regard to the carrying of firearms, as the Minister of Justice properly said, there is a question of jurisdiction. The province of Quebec has its own police force; the Dominion government has its police force. If the Dominion government wishes to authorize its men to carry firearms it has full power to do so, and the province may do the same thing. The cities, if they wish their police to be armed, must obtain the authority of the legislatures of the provinces. This is a complicated question, but I have lived in the city of Montreal for many years, and I have often wondered why the windows of the pawnshops and second hand stores were permitted to be filled with cast off revolvers selling for a dollar, a dollar and a half or two dollars. Who should control this? I have no doubt this matter has been inquired into by the Minister of Justice, but that is where the cheap revolver is obtained which is used by the man committing a crime. If a way could be found to curtail the sale of firearms except by properly authorized and responsible persons I think a great forward step would be taken.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
That is provided for in
this bill.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
The ex-Minister of Justice
tells me that this is dealt with in the bill now before us, and I am glad to hear it. With the recent fires and other occurrences in
Montreal the people have come to realize that something must be done to maintain the reputation of Canada and her citizens, and I am glad that this matter is being taken up now.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I am afraid that I must differ with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for North Bruce. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was not quite correct when he told the house that the policemen in England are not armed. It is true that for generations the members of the police forces of the old country were not allowed to carry arms, but a wave of crime has swept the old country, with bandits going around with guns, and to-day many of the metropolitan cities are arming their policemen with guns in order to combat this wave of crime. I have in my hand some statistics with regard to Vancouver, and I believe this house will be startled to learn that in the first eleven months of 1932 there were 411 armed holdups in that city. Out there life and limb are not safe. Some of the bandits are so cruel that if they hold up a man who has no money they beat him almost to death with their guns. They leave the cities in fast motor cars and go to peaceful settlements where, at the point of the gun, they hold up storekeepers and beat them up if they have not enough money to satisfy the bandits. I think it would be a dastardly crime to leave our local policemen without some means of protection against these bandits.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am heartily in support of this bill, and I should have liked to see it go even further. In connection with these holdup men I believe most of those who are caught are hardened criminals. I have a reference before me to the case of one man who admitted that he had been in one hundred holdups. How are we to deal with that sort of people if we have not some protection? I believe in drastic measures if we are to have any protection at all against these thugs and bandits, and certainly I believe in arming local policemen.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I think all members of this house hope the time will come when our policemen will not need to be armed, but when we have so many men going around the country carrying arms I think it would be a shame and a disgrace to take from our policemen their means of protecting the lives of our citizens. The hon. member for New Westminster has just referred to the holdups that took place in Vancouver during the first eleven months of 1932. These figures were
3516	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
furnished to me, and I believe to other members of the house, by Mr. Charles Delbridge, who was police commissioner of that city for the year 1932. Of the 411 holdups 324 were carried out with arms, and there were 23 attempted armed holdups. There we have over eighty per cent of the total holdups in Vancouver during that period carried out with the use of arms. Then there were twenty cases in which it was doubtful whether or not arms were used; the attempt was made to convince the victim that the holdup man was armed.
I think this all goes to prove the necessity for some legislation such as we have before us to-day. Perhaps in Vancouver our population is a little more cosmopolitan than it is in some other centres, but certainly there we have been victims of the holdup artists.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: The same thing applies to Montreal.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I agree with the provisions of this bill, and more particularly with the provision that the attorney general of the province should have the right to issue permits either to the police or to other persons carrying offensive weapons.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: In my opinion there is absolutely no reason why any civilian should carry arms. I have never owned a weapon in my life and I do not believe there is any reason for anyone to own firearms. The man w'ho carries around a firearm is a moral coward. My hon. friend from one of the British Columbia constituencies spoke of people who might carry arms inadvertently. It seems to me that if we leave that loophole in the legislation to take care of such cases everyone who is arrested under this law will endeavour to get from under by invoking that amendment. What I want to point out in connection with the Montreal case however is that this man had no opportunity to defend himself. It cannot be said that he carried arms. He was absolutely unarmed and was shot in the back.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That is not correct.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: It is.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: No. The case was heard before Magistrate Cusson who heard twenty witnesses and offered to hear as many more as might come forward, and he absolutely justified Constable Zappa in the action he had taken.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: This man was unarmed.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
He had picked
up an iron bar.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I still maintain that
he was unarmed. I absolutely agree with the contention that it is unnecessary for the police force of the country to walk around armed like soldiers in the midst of a war. It may be necessary under certain circumstances for them to carry arms, and I am not one of those who would suggest that the police force should not sometimes be armed. I should like to know however what proportion of the men who took part in holdups in Vancouver district *were natives of this country.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That does not alter the position.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: The responsibility rests with the police forces of the country to see to it that there is no unnecessary display of arms on their part. Any such display is in my opinion utterly wrong. I do not think it is a good thing to display arms to boys who, particularly at this time, have very little to do. In my opinion this legislation should if possible have some stipulations along that line.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for East Hamilton have not stated correctly the facts in connection with this

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
case as they are known in Montreal, when they say that the matter was not thoroughly investigated, and that the action of the constable was not justified. As the hon. member for Bonaventure said, after this unfortunate incident occurred the matter was taken to a judge of the sessions and some twenty witnesses were heard in regard to the warrant that was applied for by some of the friends of the man who had been killed. They wished to charge the constable with manslaughter. The result of the investigation thoroughly justified the action of the constable. This man had been visited on three occasions because he was behind in his rent and on the third occasion such action was taken as the law required. On his eviction, this disorderly crowd in Montreal-and as the hon. member for Bonaventure says, it is growing in numbers-decided to take the law into its own hands. Now, we pride ourselves in Montreal on our police force, which has properly maintained law and order and, I hope, will continue to do so. The constable in question resorted to the only means open to him when someone in the crowd picked up an iron bar to strike down his fellow constable. When they applied for a warrant charging the accused constable with manslaughter, the facts were thoroughly reviewed and it was found that he had merely attempted to protect one of his own fellow constables from being murdered by one of the crowd who had picked up this iron bar, or at any rate from sustaining severe bodily injury. He took his revolver and threatened the crowd in order to keep them back; otherwise he would shoot. They came on despite the warning, and in order to save his comrade he was obliged to shoot this man. That is the whole case, and when hon. members try to leave the impression with the house that the police in Montreal are overstepping their bounds and that murder is being committed by members of the force, I, as a member from Montreal, would ask hon. gentlemen to state all the facts and not half of them.

speechtext: How did the policeman shoot this man in the back if the man was coming on?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I was not present, but if the hon. member knows more about the judiciary of Montreal than I do I would ask him to get the facts. I am not a judge.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I simply ask my hon. friend to explain how the man happened to be shot in the back if he was coming on.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wishes to get the evidence I shall be glad to send it to him. Do I understand that he also agrees with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question. I simply want to know how the man was shot in the back if he was coming on.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
How do you
know?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Was he shot in the back?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I am absolutely in favour of the principle of this bill. The only fault I would find with it would be in regard to the undue burden that may be placed upon those whose business it is to sell these various weapons. I do believe the time has come when those whose duty it is to protect the lives and property of our citizens should themselves be safeguarded. The whole discussion with regard to the unfortunate incident that has occurred is altogether beside the question. I think that those who are charged with the enforcement of the law have heretofore shown good judgment in the discharge of their duties. Sometimes when the circumstances are such that it may be extremely difficult to determine just what line of action they ought to take, they may have to act rather quickly, but I would very much prefer quick action on the part of an officer of the law in the discharge of his duty to the quick drawing of a revolver by a thug. For that reason I will support this measure.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
To the general tenor of
this bill I do not believe there can be any serious opposition. We all agree, I believe, it is unnecessary for the ordinary civilian to have firearms in his possession or that such firearms should be bought and sold for the purpose of carrying them around for one's own protection or for use for other purposes. But if we take the view that merely passing legislation of this kind will prevent holdups and holdups with violence, we are very much mistaken, because such holdups will take place, not because those who are staging them wish to do so, but becauses the pressure of circumstances drives them to that extreme.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Just a moment. Anyone who does not agree with this point of view need not accept it; but let me point out present conditions in this country. The fact that the number of inmates in our peniten-
3518	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
tiaries and gaols is increasing by leaps and bounds is due, not to badness of heart, if you like, or to criminal tendencies on the part of our people, but to the economic position in which our people find themselves.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Of course it is. As a
matter of fact, any one who knows anything at all knows it to be the case. If we believe this legislation will prevent that sort of thing, it undoubtedly will not do anything of the kind. The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned that bandits in British Columbia not only held up people at the point of a gun, but if they found those people did not have any money, beat them up. The bandits, in doing that, are only taking a leaf out of the book of the state. The state deprives a man of the means of livelihood and then, when it finds him walking the street, it arrests him and sentences him for vagrancy.
A few years ago when I was on the Vancouver city council, I remember a young man of twenty being brought into court because he had been sleeping in a Canadian Pacific Railway freight car. When he was asked why he slept in a freight car, he said: "I had no money to buy a bed; I had no other place to sleep and I had to sleep somewhere." Despite that fact, the magistrate who, I believe, had no alternative, sentenced him to two or three months in gaol. These are the conditions we make and we shall not do away with them simply by passing legislation of this kind. I do not wish it to be understood that I am opposed to the general tenor of this measure, but I am opposed to an attempt to do by legislation something which can be done only by improving the conditions of the people.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
claim that holdups and murder are justified because of poverty?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Decidedly not.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That is what I understood him to say.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I am not saying anything of the kind. I say that people act according to the conditions in which they find themselves. If we want to make people good, we must improve conditions. That is what I say and what any person who has any understanding of psychology says.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I am heartily in accord with the general principle of the bill, but I should like to know, if the minister can tell us, precisely the position people will find

themselves in under section 118. Perhaps some of us might have to interpret the law to some of our friends. Section 118 reads:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for not less than five years who, not having a permit in form 76, has upon his person elsewhere than in his own dwelling house, shop, warehouse, counting house, or premises-
That provision might be interpreted as indicating that he might have one in his own dwelling house or upon his own premises.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: It is not an unknown thing for a man on a farm to have a revolver in his house. Would he be allowed to carry it on his own farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: On his own premises.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Suppose a farmer owns two or three quarter sections of land and has occasion to cross the road allowance or to go some distance from one to another, he would be liable, I presume, as long as he was not actually on his own premises?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I am heartily in accord with the provisions of this measure. As a matter of 'fact, I may be extreme, but I am not particularly in favour of the reduction of the penalty suggested by the minister. That, however, may be by the way. I think the minister might go a step further and have permits issued for those weapons, no matter where they are. I do not think the mere fact that an individual is allowed to have them in his house or place of business without a permit is sufficient. That provides a place for the weapon to be stored and this may be a convenience to an individual who does not want it altogether for his own protection. I should like the minister to go a step further and provide that no individual under any circumstances should be in possession o.f one of these weapons except under a permit.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I should like to oppose that because it might mean a great deal of hardship. Nearly all returned soldiers have souvenirs, such as revolvers, of which there are probably four or five thousand in this *country. To make all those people take out permits for weapons they never use, that are simply stuck away in a closet as souvenirs, is heartless.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I cannot
see that it is any hardship upon a person who desires to have on his premises a weapon, that that fact should be known by reason of

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
his holding a permit, the authorities thus being made aware of the fact. The difficulty is 'that if this bill goes through in its present form, persons who frequently use these weapons for purposes which sometimes end in murder, will keep them in their residences and take them out when they wish to use them. I do not agree with my hon. friend that it would be any terrible hardship on anyone to have to secure a permit if he wants to keep a weapon on his premises.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: The law is no good unless it has a penalty attached. People will forget to get a permit, and the first thing they know they will find themselves in the police court and a fine will be imposed. I do not think that is fair because these weapons are practically useless from a defensive standpoint. They are kept largely as souvenirs, and are probably rusty and incapable of being used.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I am very much interested in the point just raised by the hon. member for West Edmonton and under discussion by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. I think it would be a mistake to make it a crime to have a revolver on your premises or in your home. The hon. member for West Edmonton is quite logical when he says that if that were made a crime those who now have revolvers could take out permits, but the fact is, from a practical point of view, if you make it a crime it will not come to the attention of the great majority of these people who now have them.
The point raised by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is a very, very practical one. It is quite true that all over this country there are revolvers in homes, particularly in those of the men who served in the Canadian forces overseas, and they are being kept there not with any criminal intent or for any specific purpose, but as souvenirs. I know that one, of the best souvenirs a service man returning from the front could bring home, one that was coveted by them and is in the homes of many who served, is a revolver, particularly a revolver taken from the enemy. They are in the homes of nearly all the ex-service men. They are in the haversacks of the soldiers in garrets. Now if you make it a crime for them to have a revolver in their homes, unwittingly they will become criminals and be subject to the penalty. I think, therefore, it should not be made an offence to have them in a man's home. To do so would be an injustice; you would be legislating into the criminal class thousands upon thousands of innocent citizens of Canada who are guilty of no offence whatever. I strongly oppose any such amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: In regard to the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Edmonton I may say that his proposal was pretty well considered. Originally it was provided that a man might have a pistol in his home, on the theory I suppose that a Canadian's home is his castle, just like an Englishman's, and that he has the right to have anything in it and to act as he likes in his home. Certainly his first duty is to defend his own home.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: He cannot have a still in his home.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
But the consideration
that weighed in discussing this matter was the one raised by my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario. It was estimated by men who may know that there are probably a quarter of a million homes in this country where there are souvenir revolvers of the great war. One suggestion which was made by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was that all such weapons should be registered, that the number and the make of the particular pistol or revolver should be reported to the police and registered at some central office so that if it ever became necessary its ownership could be traced. However, it was considered that that involved a great deal of work, and probably of unnecessary work. After considering the matter from every angle we decided that pistols in houses and warehouses and private premises should be permitted to remain there. So long as they stay there, they are no menace to the public.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: There is no question about it that pistols in private houses or in warehouses or in any other place, so long as they remain there and are not used, are probably no menace, as the minister says, but the point that was raised by the hon. member for West Edmonton is one that had occurred to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I forgot to say that
certain of our provinces provide that you must have a permit to have such a weapon in your home; Alberta, for instance.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
That is just the point.
The danger from these revolvers, of course, is not when they are remaining unused in the home or in the warehouse, but when they are used. They can be so easily obtained and used, and then they become a danger.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: The danger is when they are loaded.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Even then the danger is
not so great unless the trigger is drawn, and the pistol used. I see that one of the places

Criminal Code-Offensive Weapons
where revolvers are frequently found is not mentioned in the act at all; that is, if a man has a revolver in a motor car. That would not be on- his person because I take it from the description of the revolver on the person that it means in a pocket or concealed somewhere in the clothing of the person, but frequently those who are travelling in motor cars and tenting out at night find it advisable to carry a revolver with them. Is it necessary that a permit should be obtained for a revolver so carried in a motor car? That would not foe covered by any of the places mentioned in the bill. The revolver would be in a vehicle in which revolvers are, unfortunately, frequently considered to be required at the present time. It would not be in the residence. Has the minister considered that phase?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

That point is perhaps
worth considering. My hon. friend from East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) who sits behind me has just suggested a few words that might cure that trouble. We might say, "has upon his person or in his possession elsewhere than in his dwelling-house." It might be in a sleigh oi' cutter or something of that kind.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Are those who take a revolver when they go hunting required to have a permit?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

The object in most of this
kind of legislation is to deter crime. I would ask the minister if before this bill was drawn up he considered an enactment such as they have in England where, when a man commits a crime and has upon his person a pistol or revolver or other weapon, five years is added to his sentence, the object being to act as a deterrent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
That is in this bill; we
provide for adding two years.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

In the old country they add
five years to the sentence, if the man is carrying a pistol or revolver.

speechtext: Will game wardens on private property who have already been appointed with the consent of the provincial government have to secure a special permit?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

speechtext:
Has the minister considered
including a weapon known as a sawed-off shotgun? Many bandits carry them around. It can be easily concealed under the coat, and is a very powerful weapon, more powerful than a revolver.

That was not specially
considered except that it comes under the general clause referring to offensive weapons. That is the clause I read when the bill was first spoken to.

The new clause 1 says, "has
upon his person.... or is carrying concealed a pistol or revolver."

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

That is framed to meet
requests which came largely from the western provinces in regard to weapons, pistols and revolvers. We have made very drastic provisions in that respect. Then, the provision in respect of offensive weapons covers "any gun or other fire arm, or air gun, or any part thereof, or any sword, sword blade, bayonet" and so on, down a long list. A sawed-off shotgun would be certainly included in that list. I did not know they were actually concealed on the person.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Yes; there have been many
cases where men have brought them in, and then drew them out. They can hold them in one hand, just like revolvers, and they should be included along with pistols and revolvers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I have never heard a
request to that effect.

speechtext:
One of the clauses
deals with the sale of weapons, and the wording is "pistol, revolver, or other offensive weapon that may be concealed upon the person." That wording would be sufficient.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
Yes. We have military regulations too.
Mr. l7OUNG: If I understand the situation aright, and the explanation the minister gave, as the law reads now and will read as amended, a man who gives or lends a rifle to his boy or permits his boy to take one out and use it commits an offence, while if he leaves the rifle around and the boy takes it and shoots, nothing can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That is right. That has been our law for ten years. As to the question of the age, I am willing to agree to any age that suits the committee.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: My objection is not so much to the age limit. Section 122 imposes the very drastic penalty of two years on anyone who under certain circumstances permits a child under sixteen years of age to shoot. I think the amendment should be to section 122.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: That is a different section altogether. It deals with a man who has been convicted of an offence.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Section 125 creates a criminal offence, punishable by a fine. But if the firearm was on the person under the circumstances laid down in section 122 the magistrate has no discretion but must sentence him to two years. So in a large number of cases where this offence under 125 is committed the offender would be sentenced to two years. I think that is going too far.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend consider that the imposition of a fine indicates a criminal offence?

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I doubt it.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: "Every one is guilty of an offence." This is the criminal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
But a criminal offence and an offence for which a fine can be imposed are very different things.
[Mr. Ross.l

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is mistaken. Section 122 says that:
Every one who has upon his person a pistol or revolver while committing any criminal offence

The case my hon. friend refers to is where a father gives or sells a shotgun-

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Or ammunition.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: -or any firearm to a boy under sixteen. The offence there has already been committed. If he was caught out shooting with his son with the firearm he would not be arrested while committing the offence. The offence mentioned in section 122 is a prior act. If the father were arrested afterwards for giving or selling the firearm to the boy that would not be the offence dealt with in section 122.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
For the sake of information
I should like to ask what military regulations permit a minor to be in possession of a rifle. I know of none.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: This law has been on the statute book for at least ten years.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I may be wrong, but I do
not know of any military regulation that permits a minor to be in charge of a rifle if the law says he shall not have one, unless it is on a campus with his cadet corps. I suppose these cadets in the schools might be out shooting somewhere with their instructor, and a policeman might come along and demand to see their permit, but I do not know of any military regulation that permits a minor to have a rifle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
The military regulations
do provide for equipment, and I assume that ammunition and rifles form part of the equipment of a soldier. Military laws are recognized in the criminal code; they include the king's orders and regulations for the army, and so on, and any act of the United Kingdom applying to His Majesty's troops in Canada, and all other orders, rules, regulations of whatever nature or kind applying to His Majesty's troops in Canada.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: Do the cadet companies come under the military regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext: I have always so understood.

subsubtopic: CARRYING PISTOL, REVOLVER OR OTHER OFFENSIVE WEAPON WITHOUT PERMIT
speechtext:
I suggest that we have
spent enough time on this section. Though I favour the age limit being placed at fourteen it seems to be the opinion of the majority of the committee that it should be twelve, so let us make it twelve and pass the section.
